From the alternatives given below, select the correct passive voice of the following sentence.

Why has Purusottam driven Parshuram out of Mainak's house?

options.text: Why has Purusottam been driven out of Mainak's house by Parshuram?
Why has Mainak been driven out of Purusottam's house by Parshuram?

questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

• **Tense Identification:** The original sentence "Why has... driven" is in the **Present Perfect** interrogative form.
 
• **Passive Voice Rule:** To convert a Present Perfect question into Passive Voice, the structure is: **Wh-word + has/have + Object + been + V3 (Past Participle) + by + Subject?**
 
• **Subject-Object Swap:** In the active voice, "Purusottam" is the subject and "Parshuram" is the object. In the passive voice, "Parshuram" must become the subject.
 
• **Verb Conversion:** The active form "has driven" becomes "has been driven" in the passive form.
 
• **Phrase Maintenance:** The prepositional phrase "out of Mainak's house" should remain attached to the action "driven" for clarity.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Why has Parshuram been driven out of Mainak's house by Purusottam?"*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Option 2:** Incorrectly introduces "Mainak" as the one being driven out, which changes the meaning of the original sentence.

questions.question:
**Select the option that expresses the given sentence in direct voice.**

He said that he had finished his work.

options.text: He said, "I have finished his work."
He said, "He has finished my work."
He said, "I have finished my work."
He said, "He had finished his work."

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Indirect Speech:** He said that he had finished his work.
 
• **Key Conversions from Indirect to Direct:**
 
 
• **Pronoun Change:**
 
 
• The third-person pronoun **"he"** (acting as the subject in the reported clause) refers to the speaker, so it changes back to the first-person **"I"** in direct speech.
 
• The possessive adjective **"his"** changes back to **"my"** to correspond with the subject "I."
 
 
 
• **Tense Change (Past Perfect to Present Perfect):**
 
 
• When converting from indirect to direct speech, the past perfect **"had finished"** is typically reverted to the present perfect **"have finished"**.
 
 
 
• **Removal of Conjunction:**
 
 
• The conjunction **"that"** is removed and replaced by a comma and quotation marks.
 
 
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"He said, 'I have finished my work.'"*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1:** Incorrect because it uses "his work," which would imply the speaker finished someone else's work.
 
• **Option 2:** Incorrect because it uses "He" and "my," suggesting a different person finished the speaker's work.
 
• **Option 4:** Incorrect because it maintains the past perfect tense and third-person pronouns, which is not how a person would naturally state their own action in direct speech.

questions.question:
Which of the following is correct regarding medium earth orbit?

I. Satellites in MEO do not need to follow specific paths around Earth.

II. MEO is very commonly used by navigation satellites.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 3 (Both I and II)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement I:** Satellites in **Medium Earth Orbit (MEO)** generally follow specific paths around Earth. This is because they are placed in stable, predictable orbits to ensure reliable operation, especially for navigation and communication purposes. *Hence, Statement I is incorrect.*
 
• **Statement II:** MEO is commonly used by **navigation satellites**. These satellites, such as those in the Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) like GPS (USA), Galileo (Europe), and GLONASS (Russia), are positioned in MEO to provide global coverage and accurate location data. *Hence, Statement II is correct.*
 
• The **altitude of MEO** typically ranges from **2,000 km to 35,786 km** above the Earth’s surface. Most navigation satellites operate at an altitude of approximately 20,000 km to ensure a balance between global coverage and reduced latency.
 
• Satellites in MEO are not stationary like geostationary satellites but instead move at high speeds. They complete an orbit around the Earth in a few hours, which allows them to provide coverage to different parts of the globe at various times.
 
• **Conclusion:** Since Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct, the correct answer is **Option 3 (Both I and II)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Medium Earth Orbit (MEO):**

 
 
• MEO lies between Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and Geostationary Orbit (GEO). Its altitude ranges from **2,000 km to 35,786 km**.
 
• It is primarily used for **navigation systems** like GPS, Galileo, and GLONASS, as well as for some communication and Earth observation purposes.
 
• Satellites in MEO have an orbital period ranging from about **2 to 12 hours**, depending on their altitude.
 
• MEO offers a balance between the wide coverage of geostationary satellites and the lower latency of low-Earth orbit satellites.
 
 
 
• **Applications of MEO Satellites:**
 
 
• **Navigation:** Systems like GPS, Galileo, and GLONASS use MEO to provide accurate location and timing services globally.
 
• **Communication:** Some communication satellites use MEO to deliver services with less delay than GEO satellites.
 
• **Earth Observation:** MEO satellites can also be used for environmental monitoring and remote sensing applications.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Orbits:**
 
 
• **Low Earth Orbit (LEO):** Altitude of **up to 2,000 km**. Commonly used for Earth observation, scientific missions, and communication constellations like Starlink.
 
• **Geostationary Orbit (GEO):** Altitude of **35,786 km**. Used for weather satellites, television broadcasting, and communication satellites.
 
• **MEO:** Positioned between LEO and GEO, providing a mix of advantages like moderate latency, global coverage, and stable orbits.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Navigation Systems in MEO:**

 
 
• **GPS:** Operated by the United States, consists of 24 to 32 satellites in MEO, at an altitude of approximately 20,200 km.
 
• **Galileo:** European GNSS system with satellites positioned in MEO at an altitude of around 23,222 km.
 
• **GLONASS:** Russian navigation system with satellites orbiting at an altitude of about 19,100 km.
 
• **BeiDou:** China’s navigation system, which also uses MEO along with GEO and LEO satellites.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of MEO:**
 
 
• Provides a balance between wide coverage (like GEO) and lower latency (like LEO).
 
• Ideal for applications requiring global coverage, such as navigation and communication.

questions.question: During the free fall of an object, as it falls, what happens to its potential energy and kinetic energy?

options.text: Both potential energy and kinetic energy decrease
Both potential energy and kinetic energy increase
Potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases
Potential energy increases while kinetic energy decreases

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Potential Energy (PE):** When an object is at a height, it possesses potential energy due to its position in a gravitational field. The formula for potential energy is **PE = mgh**, where **m** is mass, **g** is gravitational acceleration, and **h** is height. As the object falls, its height (**h**) decreases, leading to a decrease in potential energy.
 
• **Kinetic Energy (KE):** Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its motion. The formula is **KE = 1/2 mv²**, where **m** is mass and **v** is velocity. During free fall, the velocity of the object increases due to the acceleration caused by gravity, leading to an increase in kinetic energy.
 
• **Energy Conversion:** As the object falls, the decrease in potential energy is directly converted into an increase in kinetic energy, keeping the total mechanical energy constant (in the absence of air resistance).
 
• **Law of Conservation of Energy:** The total energy (sum of potential and kinetic energy) of the system remains constant throughout the free fall, as energy is merely transformed from one form to another.
 
• **Free Fall:** In free fall, the only force acting on the object is gravity. This causes the object to accelerate downward at a rate equal to the acceleration due to gravity (**9.8 m/s²** on Earth).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Potential Energy Characteristics:**

 
 
• Potential energy depends on the **position** of the object relative to a reference point.
 
• It is a form of **stored energy** and can be converted into other energy forms, such as kinetic energy.
 
• Examples: A stretched spring, water stored in a dam at a height, and an object at a certain altitude above ground.
 
 
 
• **Kinetic Energy Characteristics:**
 
 
• Kinetic energy depends on the **mass** and **velocity** of the object.
 
• It is the energy of motion and increases as the velocity of the object increases.
 
• Examples: A rolling ball, a moving car, or a falling object.
 
 
 
• **Gravitational Potential Energy:**
 
 
• This is a type of potential energy due to an object's height in a gravitational field.
 
• It is given by the formula **mgh**, where **g** is approximately **9.8 m/s²** on Earth.
 
• Gravitational potential energy decreases as the object falls closer to the ground.
 
 
 
• **Conservation of Mechanical Energy:**
 
 
• In the absence of air resistance, the total mechanical energy (PE + KE) of an object in free fall remains constant.
 
• As the object loses height (and potential energy), it gains speed (and kinetic energy), maintaining the total energy balance.
 
• This principle is crucial for understanding free fall, pendulum motion, and other energy transformations.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Air Resistance:**
 
 
• In real-world scenarios, air resistance can affect the motion of a falling object, reducing its acceleration and altering the energy conversion process.
 
• Objects in free fall under air resistance eventually reach a constant terminal velocity, where the forces of gravity and air resistance balance each other.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Free Fall Definition:** Free fall is the motion of an object under the influence of gravity alone, with no other forces acting on it (like air resistance).
 
• **Acceleration Due to Gravity:** On Earth, the acceleration due to gravity is approximately **9.8 m/s²**. This value can vary slightly depending on altitude and location.
 
• **Energy Transformation:** The transformation of potential energy into kinetic energy during free fall is a classic example of energy conversion in physics.
 
• **Applications:** Understanding free fall and energy transformation is essential in fields like **engineering**, **space exploration**, and **sports science**.

• In the year **1801**, the **Nawab of Awadh**, under pressure from the **East India Company**, was forced to cede more than half of his territory to the British.

__
 
• **Subsidiary Alliance System:**

 
 
• It was introduced by **Lord Wellesley** to bring Indian princely states under British control without direct annexation.
 
• Under this system, Indian rulers were required to station a British force in their territory and pay for its maintenance.
 
• The princely states could not ally with any other power or declare war without British permission, effectively reducing them to vassal states.
 
 
 
• **Reasons for the Cession of Awadh:**
 
 
• The British cited the **weak governance** of the Nawab and the need for administrative reforms as justification for taking over Awadh's territories.
 
• The fertile lands of Awadh were crucial for **agricultural production** and revenue generation for the East India Company.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Agreement:**
 
 
• The cession of territory weakened the **sovereignty** of the Nawab of Awadh, making him dependent on the British.
 
• The people of Awadh faced increased revenue demands and administrative changes under British rule.
 
• This event marked the beginning of a series of British interventions in Awadh, culminating in its complete annexation in **1856**.
 
 
 
• **Important Figures:**
 
 
• **Nawab Saadat Ali Khan II:** The Nawab of Awadh during the cession of territory in 1801.
 
• **Lord Wellesley:** Governor-General of India (1798–1805) who implemented the Subsidiary Alliance system.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **East India Company's Expansion:**

 
 
• By the early 19th century, the East India Company had expanded its control over large parts of India through a combination of treaties, alliances, and military conquests.
 
• The Subsidiary Alliance system was a key tool in this expansion, allowing the British to dominate Indian states without direct administration initially.
 
 
 
• **Economic Exploitation:**
 
 
• The territories ceded by Awadh were rich in resources and played a crucial role in bolstering the Company's revenues.
 
• However, the increased revenue demands placed a significant burden on the local population, leading to widespread discontent.
 
 
 
• **Annexation of Awadh (1856):**
 
 
• In 1856, the British annexed Awadh entirely, citing **misgovernance** and the Doctrine of Lapse.
 
• This annexation was one of the factors leading to the **Revolt of 1857**, as it caused widespread resentment among the people of Awadh.

questions.question: The Banking Codes and Standards of India (BCSBI) has released a "Code of Bank's Commitment to Customers (Code) in July ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2006**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Banking Codes and Standards Board of India (BCSBI)** was established to ensure fair treatment of customers by banks in India.
 
• The **"Code of Bank's Commitment to Customers"** was released by BCSBI in **July 2006**, marking a significant step towards improving customer service and transparency in banking practices.
 
• The code outlines minimum standards of banking practices that member banks must adhere to in their dealings with individual customers.
 
• The **main objective** of this code is to promote good banking practices, increase transparency, and improve customer service.
 
• This initiative was aimed at establishing trust between banks and their customers, ensuring that customers understand their rights and responsibilities in their banking relationships.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Banking Codes and Standards Board of India (BCSBI):**

 
 
• BCSBI was established in **2006** as an independent and autonomous body to ensure adherence to codes and standards by banks.
 
• Its formation was based on the recommendations of the **Committee on Procedures and Performance Audit on Public Services (CPPAPS)**, chaired by Shri S. S. Tarapore.
 
• BCSBI monitors and ensures compliance with the "Code of Bank's Commitment to Customers" and "Code of Bank's Commitment to Micro and Small Enterprises."
 
 
 
• **Code of Bank's Commitment to Customers:**
 
 
• This code sets benchmarks for banking practices and provides protection to customers by ensuring transparency in all dealings.
 
• It covers various aspects such as account opening, loan processing, customer rights, and grievance redressal mechanisms.
 
• The code also aims to inform customers about their rights and responsibilities in their banking relationships.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of the Code:**
 
 
• Ensures fair treatment of customers irrespective of their background, financial status, or profession.
 
• Provides clarity on interest rates, fees, and other charges to avoid hidden costs.
 
• Specifies timelines for various banking services, including grievance redressal.
 
• Emphasizes the importance of customer confidentiality and data protection.
 
 
 
• **Customer Protection and Awareness:**
 
 
• The code empowers customers by educating them about their rights, such as the right to be informed, the right to privacy, and the right to choose banking products.
 
• It also highlights the customer’s responsibility to provide accurate information and maintain proper documentation.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Codes by BCSBI:**

 
 
• Besides the "Code of Bank's Commitment to Customers," BCSBI also introduced the "Code of Bank’s Commitment to Micro and Small Enterprises" to support small business owners.
 
• These codes ensure that banks provide timely and adequate credit support to the micro and small enterprise (MSE) sector.
 
 
 
• **Membership of Banks:**
 
 
• Membership in BCSBI is voluntary for banks, and member banks are required to adhere to the codes and standards established by the board.
 
• Most public sector banks, private sector banks, and several foreign banks operating in India are members of BCSBI.
 
 
 
• **Grievance Redressal Mechanism:**
 
 
• The code emphasizes the need for a robust grievance redressal mechanism to address customer complaints effectively and within a specified timeframe.
 
• Customers can escalate unresolved complaints to the Banking Ombudsman if they are not satisfied with the bank's response.

questions.question: What is the total length (in km) of navigable waterways in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**14500 km**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **India has approximately 14,500 kilometers of navigable waterways**, which include rivers, canals, backwaters, and creeks. These waterways serve as a vital mode of transportation and are crucial for the economic development of the country.
 
• The inland waterways in India are regulated and developed by the **Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI)**, which was established in **1986**.
 
• Of the total 14,500 km of navigable waterways, **National Waterways (NWs) account for a significant portion**. As of now, there are **111 National Waterways** declared under the National Waterways Act, 2016.
 
• India's inland waterways are particularly prominent in states such as **Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Assam, and Kerala**, where rivers like the Ganga, Brahmaputra, and Godavari serve as major transportation routes.
 
• Inland Waterways contribute significantly to reducing transportation costs and environmental pollution, making them an eco-friendly and cost-effective mode of transport compared to road or rail.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **National Waterways in India:**

 
 
• The **Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly river system** is designated as **National Waterway 1 (NW-1)**, spanning 1,620 km from Allahabad to Haldia. It is one of the most significant waterways in India.
 
• **National Waterway 2 (NW-2)** runs along the **Brahmaputra river** in Assam, covering a length of 891 km from Dhubri to Sadiya.
 
• The **West Coast Canal in Kerala** is designated as **National Waterway 3 (NW-3)**, spanning 205 km.
 
• Other notable waterways include **NW-4 (Godavari and Krishna rivers)** and **NW-5 (Mahanadi delta rivers)**.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of Inland Waterways:**
 
 
• Inland waterways are **cost-effective** for transporting bulk goods such as coal, cement, and agricultural products.
 
• They are **environmentally friendly** as they consume less fuel and produce lower emissions compared to road and rail transport.
 
• They help in **decongesting roads and railways**, reducing the burden on existing infrastructure.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Inland Waterways Development:**
 
 
• India faces challenges such as **sedimentation**, which reduces the navigability of rivers.
 
• There is a **lack of adequate infrastructure**, such as terminals, jetties, and cargo-handling equipment.
 
• Seasonal variations in water levels, particularly during dry seasons, affect the smooth operation of inland water transport.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives:**
 
 
• The **Jal Marg Vikas Project (JMVP)**, launched in **2014**, aims to develop NW-1 (Ganga river) for commercial navigation.
 
• The **Sagarmala Programme** focuses on port-led development and improving connectivity between inland waterways and coastal areas.
 
• The **National Inland Waterways Transportation Policy** promotes the use of inland waterways as a sustainable transportation mode.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Economic Benefits:** Inland waterways reduce logistics costs, which is particularly important for India, where logistics costs are higher compared to developed nations.
 
• **Environmental Benefits:** Water transport is significantly more energy-efficient and eco-friendly compared to road and rail transport.
 
• **Examples of Cargo Transport:** Major commodities transported through inland waterways include coal, iron ore, cement, food grains, and fertilizers.
 
• **Future Potential:** If adequately developed, India’s inland waterways could handle a substantial share of the freight traffic, thus boosting economic growth.

__
 
• The Socio-Economic and Caste Census (SECC) was conducted in 2011 to gather comprehensive data on households in India.

• **SECC 2011 Objectives:**

 
 
• The primary goal was to gather socio-economic and caste data to enable the government to design and implement welfare policies effectively.
 
• It was the first-ever caste-based census conducted after 1931 in India.
 
• The SECC covered both rural and urban households, collecting data on housing, education, occupation, and socio-economic status.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of SECC 2011:**
 
 
• It was conducted using hand-held devices to digitize data collection, ensuring accuracy and reducing manual errors.
 
• For rural areas, the survey was conducted by the Ministry of Rural Development, while for urban areas, it was overseen by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs.
 
• The Registrar General of India provided technical support for the survey.
 
 
 
• **Uses of SECC Data:**
 
 
• The data was used to identify priority households for government schemes like the National Food Security Act (NFSA) and Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA).
 
• It also helped in understanding the socio-economic disparities across different regions and communities in India.
 
 
 
• **Important Figures:**
 
 
• India had a total of 640 districts in 2011 when the census was conducted. This number has since increased due to the creation of new districts in various states.
 
• The census involved extensive manpower, with enumerators visiting each household across the country.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Comparison with Previous Census:**

 
 
• The SECC 2011 was different from the Population Census 2011, as the latter focused on demographic data, while the SECC focused on socio-economic and caste data.
 
• The SECC provided data for targeted interventions, whereas the Population Census provided a general demographic overview.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in SECC 2011:**
 
 
• The survey faced challenges such as data discrepancies, privacy concerns, and political sensitivities related to caste data.
 
• Despite these challenges, the SECC 2011 remains a crucial resource for policy-making in India.
